questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I received a general information package upon arrival with different brochures with information about tourism and activities as well as information on practicalities such as bus cards or student restaurants but crucial information on courses and registration procedures at the different faculties was harder to obtain.

Some faculties (Philology) are used to receiving foreign students and there everything went pretty smooth. In some other cases no one was able to tell me what I had to do in order to get started or who I had to talk to.

Information regarding classes on the university's webpage was sometimes inaccurate or not up to date. Some professors I had contacted prior to my arrival never replied and remained unreachable either physically (because of corona restrictions) or by email. Some information I received from different contacts was also incomplete, conflicting or outright misleading. All in all obtaining clear replies on simple things such as schedules or links to online classes was sometimes challenging.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Try to quickly get in touch with the Erasmus Student Network in order to get invited to the dedicated WhatsApp group. It is a good place to ask about rooms or find roommates or hear about websites and facebook groups. 
Going through Airbnb might be the easiest solution, even though it is a bit more expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If possible, get a place that is close to the faculty (stari grad, vračar) as public transport is often unreliable.

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It took quite a while to understand how the system works in the different faculties.
In some faculties, official registration was necessary and standardized. 
In others, I lost a lot of time trying to figure out how to obtain official registrations that I could not use for anything.

In the end, the staff at the international office helped a lot with Erasmus documents which are the most important ones.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I was warmly welcomed at the international office and given information about administrative practicalities such as visa, bus card or student restaurants. For the rest, I was first redirected to staff in each of the different faculties where I was supposed to have courses. Faculties are very independent and each has its own registrations procedures so the staff at the international office could not provide more information and the staff at one faculty cannot say if the registration procedure is similar in another. There is no common system between them.

Administrative and teaching staff sometimes seemed surprised to see groups of foreign students coming to their faculty and seemed unaware of any specific registration procedures. For each of the faculties, I was told to go through standard registration procedures that required each time to provide passport copies, ID pictures and several forms only to understand later that no one knew whether this was necessary. One faculty had an IT-system for registration which was useful.
For example I had to provide in total around 8-10 ID pictures, mostly in order to make booklets (indeks) that seem useless to foreign students. 

In the end the administrative part of the registration won't help you with the academic part even if you complete everything. Just contact teachers directly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Staff at the international office was helpful with regards to Erasmus documents

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Not so successful.
Several of the courses I had chosen did not work out for different reasons. Corona restrictions made it difficult to get ahold of anyone at their office. I ended up choosing classes mostly based on how easy it was to communicate directly by email with teachers.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
My advice would be to contact staff and especially teachers by email directly as soon as your first learning agreement gets validated and double and triple check the details directly with them. If a particular teacher is slow or difficult to communicate with via email and cannot provide clear information, just consider switching to another class. 

Generally, everyone is very sweet and helpful, but under constant pressure. So it is better to be proactive and ask everyone if they have information. Most teachers are nice and will send information about practicalities for the coming semester. The situation varies a lot from faculty to faculty. Some are used to receiving foreign students and have standard procedures and IT systems etc, others not. Also things might have gotten better after corona.

Many courses will not be taught in English, even though they have a description in English on the webpage. It can be a good idea to clarify that with the teacher as well. In any case, be prepared to receive information last minute, including readings, syllabus, locations

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The weekend trips were really nice. I would also recommend renting a car and driving to other cities.
Visit especially the northern part of Serbia (Novi Sad and the region around) which has beautiful architecture.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
The northern part of Serbia, Vojvodina (Novi Sad and the region around) which has beautiful architecture.
The mountains to the east of Belgrade, on the border with Romania
Trips to Bosnia, Romania has many castles to visit.
Brutalist architecture in Novi Beograd
Zemun

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get started as early as possible with Visa procedures as they can take some time. Official stay without visa can be up to 3 months but applications for extension will not be accepted if you are too close to your end date. So make sure you get started with your application within the first 2 months after your arrival.
Apply preferably online for Visa via the official website called eUprava -
https://euprava.gov.rs/usluge/6520

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It can be a good idea to order a Revolut credit card and account before leaving to minimize conversion and transaction fees. 

Check the locations of the different faculties, some are a bit far away from the city center

The electronic card used at student restaurant gets reset to zero at the start of every month whether you have money/meals left on it or not, so just recharge it as you go.
